Dube had just returned from a tour of the United States that stretched from California to New York. His record company said Dube leaves "a great void" in the music industry after a 25-year career. It was only later that he began recording reggae tracks as a solo singer, but the genre was to dominate and define the remainder of his career. Police said Dube was attacked after dropping off two of his children in the Rosettenville area. The assailants fled with his vehicle, which crashed nearby. His death prompted an outpouring of grief and renewed anger over violent crime in South Africa.

Born Lucky Philip Dube on Aug. 3, 1964, near Ermelo in what is now Mpumalanga province, he was raised largely by his mother, Sarah. He began his recording career performing **mbaqanga**, a Zulu popular-music style, before turning to reggae in the 1980s.

Dube’s early reggae release, *Rastas Never Die*, received little exposure under apartheid, but he soon found a wide audience with songs addressing racial oppression, poverty, imprisonment, family breakdown and political violence. His 1987 album *Slave*, featuring the enduring title song about alcohol addiction, established him as a major African star.

Over a career spanning more than two decades, Dube recorded more than 20 albums in English, Zulu and Afrikaans. His best-known releases included *Prisoner*, *Captured Live*, *House of Exile*, *Victims*, *Trinity*, *Taxman*, *Serious Reggae Business*, *The Way It Is*, *Soul Taker* and his final studio album, *Respect*, released in 2006.

With a powerful voice and a stage presence shaped by both African musical traditions and Jamaican roots reggae, Dube built an audience far beyond South Africa. He toured Europe, North America, the Caribbean, Asia and across Africa, performing alongside leading international artists and helping establish African reggae as a global force. In 1996, he received a World Music Award as Africa’s best-selling recording artist.

Although frequently compared with Jamaican reggae icons, Dube gave the form a distinctly South African identity. Songs such as “Together as One,” “Prisoner,” “House of Exile,” “Different Colours/One People” and “The Way It Is” challenged apartheid and its aftermath while calling for dignity, unity and justice.

He remained wary of narrow labels, presenting reggae not simply as entertainment but as a vehicle for testimony and social criticism. His work reached listeners across racial and national boundaries during South Africa’s transition from white-minority rule to democracy.

Dube is survived by his wife, Zanele, and seven children.

His killing ended one of the most important careers in South African popular music. But his recordings—and his role in transforming reggae into a distinctly African language of resistance, reconciliation and hope—leave him among the continent’s most influential musicians.
